sectionTitle: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)
topic: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. This is called the generator effect.
An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the direction of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to apply the principles of the generator effect in a given context.
The generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.
Students should be able to:
• explain how the generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc
• draw/interpret graphs of potential difference generated in the coil against time.
Microphones use the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits.
Students should be able to explain how a moving-coil microphone works.
A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.
Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.
Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer Vp and Vs depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns.
potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V
In a step-up transformer Vs > Vp
In a step-down transformer Vs < Vp
If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.
V_s × I_s = V_p × I_p
Where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil).
power input and output, in watts, W
Students should be able to:
• explain how the effect of an alternating current in one coil in inducing a current in another is used in transformers
• explain how the ratio of the potential differences across the two coils depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each
• calculate the current drawn from the input supply to provide a particular power output

• apply the equation linking the p.d.s and number of turns in the two coils of a transformer to the currents and the power transfer involved, and relate these to the advantages of power transmission at high potential differences.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The core is treated throughout exactly as the specification treats it: a piece of iron, chosen because iron is easily magnetised, whose job is to carry the changing magnetic field from the primary coil to the secondary coil. No concept, misconception, question stem, option or rationale in this section mentions laminations, eddy currents, hysteresis or any other named cause of core loss. Where efficiency appears it appears only in the conditional form the specification uses - if a transformer were 100% efficient the power output would equal the power input - and no question asks why a real transformer falls short of that, so no student can be credited or penalised for knowing about eddy currents. Questions asking why iron is used are answerable in full by 'iron is easily magnetised', and questions asking why transformers need an alternating supply are answerable in full by 'the magnetic field in the core must keep changing to induce a potential difference in the secondary coil'.

concepts.definition: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor forms part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in it. This is called the generator effect.

The potential difference that appears across the ends of a conductor because of relative movement between the conductor and a magnetic field, or because the magnetic field around the conductor is changing. It exists across the ends of the conductor whether or not the circuit is complete.

The current that flows when a conductor with an induced potential difference across it is part of a complete circuit. No cell is needed: the generator effect is itself the source of the potential difference that drives the current.

An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change - either the movement of the conductor or the change in the magnetic field. This is why work has to be done to keep a generator turning, and why a magnet moved near a closed coil feels a resisting force.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The induced potential difference and induced current are made larger by moving the conductor or magnet faster, by using a stronger magnet, and by using more turns of wire on the coil. What all three share is that they increase how rapidly the magnetic field through the coil changes.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the direction of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The direction of the induced potential difference and induced current is reversed by reversing the direction of motion of the conductor or magnet, and by reversing the poles of the magnet, that is by reversing the direction of the magnetic field.

A generator in which a coil rotating in a magnetic field is connected to the external circuit through two slip rings, so the connections never swap over. The current in the external circuit therefore reverses every half turn: an alternator generates ac.

A generator in which a coil rotating in a magnetic field is connected to the external circuit through a split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn. The current in the external circuit therefore never reverses: a dynamo generates dc.

Two continuous rings, one connected to each end of the rotating coil, that keep each end of the coil permanently connected to the same side of the external circuit. Slip rings are what make an alternator produce ac.

A single ring split into two halves, one connected to each end of the rotating coil. Every half turn the halves change contacts, swapping which end of the coil feeds which side of the external circuit, so the output never reverses. This is what makes a dynamo produce dc.

concepts.term: Potential difference-time graph for an alternator
concepts.definition: A graph that alternates between positive and negative values, crossing zero twice per rotation. The peaks occur when the coil is moving across the field lines fastest; the zeros occur when the coil is moving along the field lines.

concepts.term: Potential difference-time graph for a dynamo
concepts.definition: A graph of humps that all lie on the same side of the time axis, touching zero twice per rotation but never going negative, because the commutator swaps the connections at the moment the coil output would otherwise reverse.

concepts.term: Effect of faster rotation on the output graph
concepts.definition: Turning the coil faster makes the peaks taller and the humps narrower: the induced potential difference is larger and its frequency is higher, so more cycles fit into the same time.

A device that uses the generator effect to turn sound into an electrical signal. Pressure variations in the sound wave move a diaphragm, the diaphragm moves a coil over a permanent magnet, and the movement of the coil in the magnetic field induces a potential difference that varies with the pressure variations.

A device consisting of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic field in the core, and that changing field induces an alternating potential difference in the secondary coil.

The core linking the two coils of a transformer. Iron is used because it is easily magnetised, so it carries the changing magnetic field from the primary coil to the secondary coil. It carries magnetic field, not current: there is no electrical connection between the coils.

The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils, Vp and Vs, depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns: Vp / Vs = np / ns, with potential difference in volts, V.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary, so that Vs > Vp. Used at a power station to raise the potential difference for transmission.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary, so that Vs < Vp. Used near consumers to bring the transmission potential difference down to a usable value.

If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs x Is = Vp x Ip, where Vs x Is is the power output at the secondary coil and Vp x Ip is the power input at the primary coil, with power in watts, W.

For a given power, raising the potential difference lowers the current, and a smaller current in the transmission cables wastes less energy by heating. This is why the National Grid uses step-up transformers before transmission and step-down transformers afterwards.

misconceptions.question: A coil is connected only to a sensitive ammeter. There is no cell in the circuit. Can a current flow?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Moving a magnet near the coil induces a potential difference across the coil, and because the circuit is complete a current is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no current, because a circuit needs a cell or battery to drive one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every circuit a student has built before this topic contains a cell, and 'the cell pushes the charge round' has been the working rule for two years. Nothing in that rule prepares them for a source of potential difference that is a piece of moving metal.
misconceptions.correction: The generator effect is itself a source of potential difference. Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field, or a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, induces a potential difference across the ends of the conductor, and no cell is needed. That is how every power station produces its electricity.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is held stationary inside a coil that is part of a complete circuit. Is there an induced current?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nothing is changing, so no potential difference is induced and no current flows.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a current, because the magnet is inside the coil and its field passes through the turns.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch on to the presence of the magnetic field rather than to its change, because in every other topic a field simply being there is enough to produce an effect.
misconceptions.correction: It is the change that induces the potential difference, not the field itself. The conductor must move relative to the field, or the field around the conductor must change. A magnet at rest inside a coil produces a steady field and therefore no induced potential difference at all.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed towards a coil. Does the magnetic field made by the induced current help or hinder the magnet?
misconceptions.correct: It hinders it. The induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the movement of the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: It helps it, so the magnet is pulled in and speeds up as it approaches the coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The idea that a magnet and a coil attract each other is well established from electromagnets, and nothing in the student's picture suggests the coil should push back.
misconceptions.correction: An induced current always generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change - here the approach of the magnet. If it helped the magnet instead, the magnet would accelerate for ever and energy would be created from nothing.

misconceptions.question: What decides how big the induced potential difference is when a magnet is moved into a coil?
misconceptions.correct: How rapidly the field through the coil changes: the speed of the movement, the strength of the magnet and the number of turns.
misconceptions.misconception: How long the magnet spends inside the coil - leaving it there longer gives a bigger reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the everyday idea that doing something for longer produces more of the result, and confuse a large induced potential difference with a long-lasting one.
misconceptions.correction: Only the rate of change matters. Moving the magnet faster gives a bigger induced potential difference for a shorter time; leaving the magnet at rest inside the coil gives nothing at all, however long it stays there.

misconceptions.question: Does adding more turns to the coil change the size of the induced potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. More turns on the coil gives a larger induced potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: No. Extra turns only add resistance, so they can only make the reading smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only property of a coil students have used before is its resistance, so extra wire is read purely as extra resistance rather than as extra conductor in the changing field.
misconceptions.correction: The number of turns is one of the factors that affects the size of the induced potential difference. Each turn has a potential difference induced across it and the turns are in series, so more turns means a larger induced potential difference overall.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil and the meter deflects to the right. What happens if the magnet is pulled straight back out?
misconceptions.correct: The meter deflects to the left: reversing the movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: The meter deflects to the right again, because it is the same magnet and the same coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the induced current as a property of the pairing of magnet and coil rather than as something set by the direction of the change.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of the induced potential difference is reversed by reversing the direction of movement, and also by reversing the poles of the magnet. Pushing in and pulling out are opposite changes, so they give opposite deflections.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the induced current if the magnet is turned round so the south pole enters the coil first?
misconceptions.correct: The induced current flows the other way round the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing changes, because the speed of the magnet is what sets the direction of the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed has just been learned as the factor controlling size, and students carry it over to direction as well because it is the variable they have been thinking hardest about.
misconceptions.correction: Speed affects only the size of the induced potential difference. Its direction depends on the direction of the movement and on the direction of the magnetic field, so reversing the poles reverses the induced current.

misconceptions.question: Which generator produces alternating current, the alternator or the dynamo?
misconceptions.correct: The alternator produces ac; the dynamo produces dc.
misconceptions.misconception: The dynamo produces ac and the alternator produces dc.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both machines are coils spinning in magnetic fields and look nearly identical in diagrams, so the two names get attached to the wrong outputs. 'Dynamo' also sounds to students like the more powerful, mains-like device.
misconceptions.correction: The names go with the connections. An alternator uses slip rings, which never swap the connections, so its output alternates. A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn, so its output is dc.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between the connections used in an alternator and in a dynamo?
misconceptions.correct: An alternator uses two slip rings; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator.
misconceptions.misconception: An alternator uses a split-ring commutator, because the commutator is what makes the output alternate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'commutator' is associated with alternating output because 'commute' suggests going back and forth, and because the commutator is first met in the motor topic where it is described as reversing something.
misconceptions.correction: The commutator reverses the connections every half turn, which cancels the reversal in the coil and gives an output that never changes sign. That is dc, and it belongs to the dynamo. Slip rings leave the reversal in place and give the alternator its ac.

misconceptions.question: What does a graph of the potential difference generated by a dynamo against time look like?
misconceptions.correct: A series of humps all on the same side of the time axis, touching zero twice each rotation but never going negative.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave that goes equally far above and below the time axis, like the mains supply.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every potential difference-time graph students have drawn in this topic so far has been a sine wave, and the dynamo graph is drawn from the same rotating coil, so the negative half is expected to be there.
misconceptions.correction: The commutator swaps the connections at exactly the moment the coil's output would reverse, so the negative half of each cycle is flipped up. The graph touches zero but never crosses it.

misconceptions.question: A generator's coil is turned twice as fast. How does the output graph change?
misconceptions.correct: The peaks become taller and the cycles become shorter: both the size and the frequency of the output increase.
misconceptions.misconception: The cycles get closer together but the peaks stay exactly the same height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Frequency is the visible change on the screen of an oscilloscope, and students read the graph as a picture of timing only, forgetting that speed is also a factor controlling the size of the induced potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: Turning the coil faster increases how rapidly the field through it changes, so the induced potential difference is larger as well as more frequent. The peaks get taller and the humps get narrower at the same time.

misconceptions.question: How does a moving-coil microphone work?
misconceptions.correct: Pressure variations in the sound wave move a diaphragm and the coil attached to it. The coil moves in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet, so a potential difference is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: A current is sent through the coil, and the coil pushes on the magnet to make the diaphragm move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The microphone and the loudspeaker share almost the same diagram, and the loudspeaker version - the motor effect - is usually taught first, so the same explanation is offered for both.
misconceptions.correction: A microphone runs the loudspeaker backwards. It uses the generator effect, not the motor effect: sound moves the coil, and the movement of the coil in the magnetic field induces a potential difference which varies with the pressure variations in the sound wave.

misconceptions.question: What actually induces the potential difference in a moving-coil microphone?
misconceptions.correct: The movement of the coil in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure of the sound wave squeezing the wire and pushing the charges along it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Sound makes electricity' is remembered without a mechanism, and pressure acting directly on the wire is the most concrete story available.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure alone induces nothing. The sound wave moves the diaphragm, the diaphragm moves the coil, and it is the movement of that coil relative to the magnetic field that induces the potential difference. Louder sound moves the coil further and faster, so the induced potential difference is larger.

misconceptions.question: A transformer is connected to a steady dc supply. What appears across the secondary coil?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing, once the current has settled. A steady current gives an unchanging magnetic field, so nothing is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: A steady dc output, stepped up or down by the turns ratio in the usual way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The turns ratio equation is memorised as a rule about voltages and turns, with no mention of change in it, so it seems to apply to any supply at all.
misconceptions.correction: A transformer needs an alternating current in the primary coil so that the magnetic field in the core keeps changing. Only a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference in the secondary coil; with steady dc the output is zero.

misconceptions.question: How does energy get from the primary coil to the secondary coil of a transformer?
misconceptions.correct: The alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the core, and that changing field induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron core carries the current across from the primary coil to the secondary coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The core is drawn as a solid loop joining the two coils, and iron is known to be a good conductor, so it reads as a wire connecting them.
misconceptions.correction: There is no electrical connection between the coils. The core carries magnetic field, not current. It is the changing magnetic field in the core that induces the potential difference in the secondary coil.

misconceptions.question: Why is the core of a transformer made of iron?
misconceptions.correct: Because iron is easily magnetised.
misconceptions.misconception: Because iron conducts electricity well, so it lets the current pass through easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron is filed under 'metal, therefore good conductor', and the electrical property is the one students have been asked about far more often than the magnetic one.
misconceptions.correction: The core's job is magnetic, not electrical. Iron is used because it is easily magnetised, so the changing magnetic field made by the primary coil is carried effectively round to the secondary coil.

misconceptions.question: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 400 on the secondary. How do the potential differences compare?
misconceptions.correct: Vs is four times Vp, because Vp / Vs = np / ns.
misconceptions.misconception: Vs is a quarter of Vp, because more turns share the potential difference out between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled without its labels attached, and the everyday picture of a quantity being shared among more things pulls the answer the wrong way.
misconceptions.correction: Vp / Vs = np / ns, so the coil with more turns has the larger potential difference. With four times as many turns on the secondary, Vs is four times Vp - a step-up transformer.

misconceptions.question: A step-up transformer raises the potential difference. What does it do to the power?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing. If it were 100% efficient the power output would equal the power input.
misconceptions.misconception: It raises the power too, since raising the potential difference gives more energy each second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step up' is heard as 'make bigger' applied to everything, and power and potential difference are not yet clearly separated in the student's mind.
misconceptions.correction: A transformer changes potential difference and current together, not power. If transformers were 100% efficient the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs x Is = Vp x Ip.

misconceptions.question: In a step-up transformer, what happens to the current in the secondary coil?
misconceptions.correct: It is smaller than the primary current, because the power output cannot exceed the power input.
misconceptions.misconception: It is larger, because stepping up increases the potential difference and the current together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Potential difference and current are usually seen rising together in Ohm's law problems, so they are expected to move together here as well.
misconceptions.correction: Vs x Is = Vp x Ip for a 100% efficient transformer, so if Vs is bigger than Vp then Is must be smaller than Ip. Stepping the potential difference up steps the current down, which is exactly why it is done before transmission.

misconceptions.question: If a transformer were 100% efficient, what would be equal?
misconceptions.correct: The electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.
misconceptions.misconception: The output potential difference would equal the input potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: '100% efficient' is read as 'nothing changes', and potential difference is the quantity written on the transformer in the question, so it is the one assumed to be conserved.
misconceptions.correction: Efficiency is about energy and power, not about potential difference. A 100% efficient transformer still changes the potential difference; what stays the same is the power, so Vs x Is = Vp x Ip.

misconceptions.question: Why is electrical power transmitted across the country at a very high potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: Because for a given power a higher potential difference means a smaller current, and a smaller current wastes less energy heating the cables.
misconceptions.misconception: Because a higher potential difference lowers the resistance of the transmission cables.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any explanation that reduces heating gets attached to resistance, since resistance is the quantity students associate with wasted energy in a wire.
misconceptions.correction: The resistance of the cables is fixed by what they are made of and how long and thick they are. What the step-up transformer changes is the current: for the same power, a higher potential difference needs a smaller current, and less energy is wasted heating the cables.

misconceptions.question: Does a transformer change the frequency of the supply?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the potential difference and current change; the frequency of the output is the same as the input.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, a step-up transformer raises the frequency along with the potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step up' is applied to every property of the supply at once, and frequency is the other number students associate with an ac supply.
misconceptions.correction: The magnetic field in the core changes in step with the primary current, so the secondary output alternates at exactly the same frequency. Only the size of the potential difference and current is changed by the turns ratio.

misconceptions.question: What unit is the power input or output of a transformer given in?
misconceptions.correct: Watts, W.
misconceptions.misconception: Volt-amps or amps, since the equation multiplies a potential difference by a current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation Vs x Is = Vp x Ip is remembered as a pair of symbols rather than as an expression for power, so its unit is built out of the symbols instead of recalled.
misconceptions.correction: Vs x Is is the electrical power output and Vp x Ip is the electrical power input, and power input and output are measured in watts, W.

misconceptions.question: In Vs x Is = Vp x Ip, which side is the power output?
misconceptions.correct: Vs x Is, the secondary coil, is the power output; Vp x Ip, the primary coil, is the power input.
misconceptions.misconception: Vp x Ip is the output, because the primary coil is the one that comes first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Primary' is heard as 'main' or 'first, therefore the important one', and the supply is often drawn on the right of the diagram, so the labels get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The primary coil is the one connected to the supply, so Vp x Ip is the power input. The secondary coil is the one feeding the load, so Vs x Is is the power output.

mcqs.stem: A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil of wire that is connected to a sensitive ammeter. There is no cell anywhere in the circuit. What does the ammeter show while the magnet is moving inwards?

options.text: A current, because the magnetic field through the coil is changing
options.rationale: A change in the magnetic field around a conductor induces a potential difference, and because the circuit is complete a current is induced.

options.text: No current, since the circuit contains no cell to drive one
options.rationale: Applies the rule that a current needs a driving cell, and no cell is visible in this circuit.

options.text: No current until the magnet is at rest inside the coil
options.rationale: Treats the magnet being inside the coil, rather than its movement, as the source of the current.

options.text: A current only in the turns the magnet has passed
options.rationale: Imagines the effect as local to the part of the coil the magnet is beside, rather than a potential difference across the whole coil.

mcqs.stem: A straight wire is connected to a sensitive voltmeter and held between the poles of a strong magnet. In which situation is a potential difference induced across the ends of the wire?

options.text: While the wire is held still in the strong magnetic field
options.rationale: Takes the presence of a strong field as sufficient, ignoring that nothing is changing.

options.text: While the wire is moved across the magnetic field lines
options.rationale: Moving the conductor relative to the magnetic field induces a potential difference across its ends.

options.text: While the wire is moved along the field lines, parallel to them
options.rationale: Moving parallel to the lines does not change the field through the circuit, so nothing is induced; the student sees only that the wire is moving.

options.text: Only while a cell is connected in that circuit
options.rationale: Assumes a potential difference must come from a supply rather than from the generator effect.

mcqs.stem: The north pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil, and a current is induced in the coil. What does the magnetic field produced by that induced current do?

options.text: It pulls the magnet inwards, so the magnet speeds up as it enters
options.rationale: Assumes coils and magnets always attract, so the induced field is imagined helping the motion.

options.text: It has no effect on the magnet, being far too weak to matter
options.rationale: Dismisses the induced field as negligible, which removes the need to think about opposition at all.

options.text: It opposes the magnet's approach, pushing back on it
options.rationale: An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, here the movement of the magnet towards the coil.

options.text: It cancels the magnet's field, leaving none in the coil
options.rationale: Reads 'opposes' as 'exactly cancels', which would leave no changing field and so no induced current at all.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pulled away from a coil that forms part of a complete circuit. The student notices that the magnet resists being pulled away. Why?

options.text: Because the copper wire of the coil is itself magnetic material
options.rationale: Attributes the force to the wire being attracted as iron would be, rather than to the induced current.

options.text: Because the field of the induced current helps the magnet leave
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the opposition backwards, which would mean the magnet was pulled out rather than held back.

options.text: Because a magnet's own field always pulls back on nearby wire
options.rationale: Invents a permanent attraction between magnet and wire, so the resistance would be felt even with the circuit broken.

options.text: Because the induced current's field opposes the change
options.rationale: An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, so removing the magnet is resisted.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is moved into a coil connected to a data logger. Which change on its own would increase the size of the induced potential difference?

options.text: Using a lead of thicker copper between the coil and logger
options.rationale: Changes the circuit's resistance slightly but not the rate at which the field through the coil changes.

options.text: Moving the same magnet into the coil at a much higher speed
options.rationale: Speed of movement is one of the factors that affects the size of the induced potential difference.

options.text: Winding fewer turns of wire onto the coil than before
options.rationale: Treats extra turns as extra resistance only, so removing turns is expected to help.

options.text: Holding the magnet inside the coil for a longer time
options.rationale: Confuses a large induced potential difference with a long-lasting one.

mcqs.stem: Two identical coils are used in the same experiment. Coil A has 200 turns and coil B has 800 turns. The same magnet is moved into each at the same speed. What is observed?

options.text: Both coils give exactly the same induced potential difference
options.rationale: Holds that only the magnet and its speed matter, so the number of turns is irrelevant.

options.text: Coil B gives the smaller reading, as it has more resistance
options.rationale: Reads the extra wire purely as extra resistance, which is the only property of a coil met before this topic.

options.text: Coil B gives the larger induced potential difference
options.rationale: The number of turns on the coil is one of the factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference.

options.text: Coil A gives a larger reading because its wire is shorter
options.rationale: Assumes a short conductor must give the bigger effect, borrowing from resistance reasoning.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil and the meter needle swings to the right. The magnet is then pulled straight back out at the same speed. What does the needle do?

options.text: It swings to the right again, as it is the same magnet and coil
options.rationale: Treats the deflection as a fixed property of this magnet and coil rather than of the direction of the change.

options.text: It stays at zero, because pulling out cannot induce anything
options.rationale: Associates induction only with the magnet approaching, not with any change in the field.

options.text: It swings to the left, the opposite way to before
options.rationale: Reversing the direction of movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference.

options.text: It swings right, then left, twice for the one movement
options.rationale: Expects a double deflection from a single change, confusing this with an alternating output.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil north pole first and the induced current flows clockwise round the coil. The magnet is turned round and pushed in south pole first at the same speed. What happens?

options.text: The current flows anticlockwise round the coil
options.rationale: Reversing the direction of the magnetic field reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.

options.text: The current still flows clockwise but is now much larger
options.rationale: Keeps the direction fixed and instead changes the size, which is what speed would do.

options.text: The current still flows clockwise, since the speed is the same
options.rationale: Treats speed as the factor that sets direction, when speed only affects size.

options.text: No current flows at all with the south pole leading
options.rationale: Assumes only a north pole can induce a current, treating the north pole as the active one.

mcqs.stem: An aircraft with metal wings flies horizontally through the Earth's magnetic field. A voltmeter is connected between the wing tips. What does it read, and why?

options.text: Zero, because the wings are not connected to a power supply
options.rationale: Requires a cell before any potential difference can exist, ignoring the generator effect.

options.text: Zero, because metal wings are not magnetic like iron is
options.rationale: Confuses being a magnetic material with being a conductor moving through a field.

options.text: A small reading, since a conductor is moving through a field
options.rationale: An electrical conductor moving relative to a magnetic field has a potential difference induced across its ends.

options.text: A reading only while the aircraft is climbing or turning
options.rationale: Assumes a change of direction is needed, when steady motion across the field lines is enough.

mcqs.stem: A student states that an alternator generates ac and a dynamo generates dc. Which statement about the connections is correct?

options.text: The alternator uses a split ring; the dynamo uses slip rings
options.rationale: Swaps the two connection types, a very common recall error.

options.text: Both machines use slip rings, but the dynamo spins much faster
options.rationale: Explains the difference by speed rather than by how the coil is connected to the circuit.

options.text: Both use a split-ring commutator, wired the opposite way round
options.rationale: Keeps the commutator for both and invents a wiring difference instead.

options.text: The alternator uses slip rings; the dynamo uses a split ring
options.rationale: Slip rings never swap the connections, so the output alternates; the split-ring commutator swaps them every half turn, giving dc.

mcqs.stem: A coil is rotated at a steady rate between the poles of a magnet. Why is a potential difference generated at all?

options.text: Because the coil is cutting across the magnetic field lines as it turns
options.rationale: The conductor is moving relative to the magnetic field, which is the generator effect.

options.text: Because spinning the coil makes it heat up and release charge
options.rationale: Substitutes a thermal story for the generator effect.

options.text: Because the magnet pushes current along the wire of the coil
options.rationale: Makes the field itself the driver, rather than the relative movement.

options.text: Because the coil is connected to the circuit through rings
options.rationale: Confuses the connection method, which sets ac or dc, with the source of the potential difference.

mcqs.stem: In a dynamo, what job does the split-ring commutator do?

options.text: It keeps the coil turning by reversing the current in it each half turn
options.rationale: Describes the commutator's role in a motor, where it does keep the coil turning.

options.text: It swaps the connections every half turn, so the output stays dc
options.rationale: The commutator changes contacts as the coil output would reverse, so the external current never changes direction.

options.text: It makes the output alternate, which is why we call it commuting
options.rationale: Reads 'commutator' as meaning 'goes back and forth', giving it the slip rings' effect.

options.text: It stores charge between rotations to smooth out the humps
options.rationale: Attributes a capacitor's smoothing role to the commutator.

mcqs.stem: An alternator and a dynamo have identical coils and magnets and are turned at the same rate. How do their outputs differ?

options.text: Only the alternator's output reverses direction each half turn
options.rationale: The alternator's slip rings leave the reversal in place, giving ac; the dynamo's commutator removes it, giving dc.

options.text: Only the dynamo's output reverses, because it is the ac machine
options.rationale: Attaches the ac output to the wrong machine.

options.text: The dynamo's output is steady, never rising or falling
options.rationale: Reads 'dc' as 'constant', when a dynamo's output rises and falls in humps.

options.text: The alternator's output is larger but does not reverse
options.rationale: Keeps the ac property away from the alternator and swaps in a size difference instead.

mcqs.stem: In an alternator, why does the output reverse direction twice during every complete rotation of the coil?

options.text: Because each side of the coil moves up through the field, then down
options.rationale: Each side of the coil reverses its direction of movement relative to the field every half turn, reversing the induced potential difference.

options.text: Because the magnet's poles swap over twice in each rotation
options.rationale: Makes the fixed magnet do the reversing rather than the moving coil.

options.text: Because the slip rings swap the connections every half turn
options.rationale: Gives the slip rings the commutator's swapping action; slip rings keep the same contacts throughout.

options.text: Because the coil stops for an instant twice per rotation
options.rationale: Confuses the two moments when the output is zero with the coil actually halting.

mcqs.stem: A graph of the potential difference generated by a dynamo is plotted against time. What does it look like?

options.text: A wave going equally far above and below the time axis
options.rationale: Draws the alternator's graph, since every rotating-coil graph met so far has had a negative half.

options.text: A horizontal straight line at one fixed positive value
options.rationale: Reads dc as meaning a constant output, ignoring that the coil's speed across the field lines varies.

options.text: Humps on one side of the axis, touching zero but not crossing
options.rationale: The commutator flips the would-be negative half up, so the graph reaches zero twice per rotation but never goes negative.

options.text: A sloping line that climbs steadily as the coil keeps turning
options.rationale: Treats the output as accumulating over time rather than varying within each rotation.

mcqs.stem: An alternator's coil is turned twice as fast as before. How does the potential difference-time graph change?

options.text: The cycles get shorter but the peaks keep exactly the same height
options.rationale: Reads the graph as showing timing only, forgetting that speed also affects the size of the induced potential difference.

options.text: The peaks get taller and the cycles get shorter
options.rationale: Faster rotation changes the field through the coil more rapidly, so the induced potential difference is both larger and more frequent.

options.text: The peaks get taller but each cycle lasts just as long as before
options.rationale: Changes the size only, keeping the frequency fixed even though the coil turns faster.

options.text: The graph stops crossing zero and becomes a set of humps
options.rationale: Confuses a change of speed with a change from slip rings to a commutator.

mcqs.stem: How does a microphone use the generator effect?

options.text: Pressure variations in the sound wave are converted into current variations
options.rationale: Microphones use the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits.

options.text: Variations in the current are converted into pressure variations in air
options.rationale: Describes a loudspeaker, which uses the motor effect, and runs the microphone backwards.

options.text: The sound wave heats the coil, and the hot coil then passes current
options.rationale: Substitutes a thermal mechanism for the generator effect.

options.text: The sound wave magnetises the diaphragm, which stores the signal
options.rationale: Invents a magnetising step and leaves out the movement of the coil in the field.

mcqs.stem: In a moving-coil microphone, what is it that actually induces the potential difference?

options.text: The sound wave pressing directly on the wire of the coil
options.rationale: Has pressure itself pushing the charges along, with no movement in a magnetic field.

options.text: The coil moving in the field of the permanent magnet
options.rationale: The diaphragm moves the coil, and movement of the coil relative to the magnetic field induces the potential difference.

options.text: A current sent through the coil pushing on the magnet
options.rationale: Describes the motor effect used in a loudspeaker rather than the generator effect.

options.text: The magnet vibrating in step with the sound wave
options.rationale: Moves the wrong part: in a moving-coil microphone the magnet is fixed and the coil moves.

mcqs.stem: What does a basic transformer consist of?

options.text: A primary coil and a secondary coil joined by a length of copper wire
options.rationale: Keeps an electrical connection between the coils, which a transformer does not have.

options.text: A single coil of wire wound tightly around an iron core
options.rationale: Leaves out the second coil, so there is nothing for the changing field to induce a potential difference in.

options.text: A primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of a basic transformer.

options.text: Two coils wound on a core of plastic to insulate them
options.rationale: Chooses the core material for electrical insulation rather than for being easily magnetised.

mcqs.stem: Why is the core of a transformer made of iron?

options.text: Because iron conducts electricity well and carries the current across
options.rationale: Gives the core an electrical job, when its job is to carry the changing magnetic field.

options.text: Because iron is strong enough to hold the heavy coils in place
options.rationale: Chooses a mechanical reason, which is plausible from the look of a transformer but not the physics.

options.text: Because iron is easily magnetised
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives.

options.text: Because iron does not get hot when a current flows in it
options.rationale: Invents an electrical property of iron and again treats the core as part of the circuit.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 2500 turns on the secondary coil. How do the potential differences across the coils compare?

options.text: Vs is five times Vp, since Vp / Vs = np / ns
options.rationale: With five times as many turns on the secondary, the secondary potential difference is five times the primary.

options.text: Vs is one fifth of Vp, as the turns share it out
options.rationale: Inverts the ratio, using the everyday idea that more things share a quantity out.

options.text: Vs equals Vp, since the same core links them
options.rationale: Assumes the core simply passes the potential difference straight through unchanged.

options.text: Vs is 2000 V more than Vp, from the extra turns
options.rationale: Treats the relationship as a difference in turns rather than a ratio.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 800 turns on the primary coil and 40 turns on the secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary coil is 240 V. What is the potential difference across the secondary coil?

options.rationale: Subtracts the turns instead of taking their ratio, giving 240 x 760/800.
Uses the ratio upside down, multiplying by 800/40 instead of dividing.
Vp / Vs = np / ns, so Vs = 240 x 40/800 = 12 V.

options.text: 6 V
options.rationale: Halves the correct value, a slip from using 20 turns per volt the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: In the transformer equation Vp / Vs = np / ns, what are Vp and Vs measured in, and what are np and ns?

options.text: Vp and Vs in amps; np and ns are the numbers of turns
options.rationale: Attaches the wrong unit to the potential differences.

options.text: Vp and Vs in volts; np and ns are the lengths of the coils
options.rationale: Gets the unit right but replaces turns with a length, which the equation does not use.

options.text: Vp and Vs in volts; np and ns are the numbers of turns
options.rationale: Potential difference, Vp and Vs, is measured in volts, V, and np and ns are the numbers of turns on each coil.

options.text: Vp and Vs in watts; np and ns are the currents in each coil
options.rationale: Mixes in the power unit and replaces the turns with currents.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a step-up transformer?

options.text: Vs > Vp, with more turns on the secondary coil
options.rationale: In a step-up transformer the secondary potential difference is greater than the primary.

options.text: Vs < Vp, with fewer turns on the secondary coil
options.rationale: Describes a step-down transformer, swapping the two definitions.

options.text: Vs > Vp, with more turns on the primary coil instead
options.rationale: Gets the direction right but attaches the extra turns to the wrong coil.

options.text: Vs > Vp and Is > Ip, as both are stepped up together
options.rationale: Raises the current alongside the potential difference, which would create power from nothing.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is used to bring 230 V down to 12 V for a lamp. What kind of transformer is it, and how are its coils wound?

options.text: Step-down, with fewer turns on the primary than the secondary
options.rationale: Names it correctly but inverts which coil carries more turns.

options.text: Step-up, since a lamp needs its supply raised to work well
options.rationale: Assumes any transformer feeding a device must raise the supply.

options.text: Step-down, with fewer turns on the secondary coil than the primary
options.rationale: In a step-down transformer Vs < Vp, and the coil with fewer turns has the smaller potential difference.

options.text: Step-down, with equal turns on the two coils of the transformer
options.rationale: Keeps the name but removes the turns ratio that produces the change.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is assumed to be 100% efficient. Which quantity is the same on both sides of it?

options.text: The potential difference across each of the two coils
options.rationale: Reads 100% efficient as meaning nothing changes at all, which would make the transformer pointless.

options.text: The electrical power, so the output equals the input
options.rationale: If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.

options.text: The current in the primary and in the secondary coil
options.rationale: Picks the other quantity in the power equation, which also changes.

options.text: The number of turns on each of the two coils
options.rationale: Confuses a statement about energy with a statement about construction.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is 100% efficient. The primary coil takes 3 A at 200 V. The secondary coil supplies a device at 25 V. What is the current in the secondary coil?

options.rationale: Vs x Is = Vp x Ip, so Is = 200 x 3 / 25 = 24 A.
Uses the ratio upside down, giving 25 x 3 / 200, so the current falls as the potential difference falls.
Quotes the power input, 200 x 3 = 600 W, as though it were the current.

options.text: 8 A
options.rationale: Uses the turns-style ratio 200/25 alone and forgets to include the primary current.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Vs x Is = Vp x Ip, which side is the electrical power output, and what unit is it in?

options.text: Vp x Ip is the output, because the primary coil comes first
options.rationale: Reads 'primary' as 'main', so the input and output labels are swapped.

options.text: Vs x Is is the power output, measured in watts, W
options.rationale: Vs x Is is the power output at the secondary coil and Vp x Ip is the power input at the primary, with power in watts.

options.text: Vs x Is is the output, and it is measured in volt-amps
options.rationale: Builds the unit out of the symbols instead of recalling that power is in watts.

options.text: Both sides are outputs, one for each coil of the transformer
options.rationale: Loses the distinction between the supply side and the load side.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is connected to a steady direct current supply instead of an alternating one. What is the potential difference across the secondary coil once the current has settled?

options.text: A steady output, stepped up or down by the turns ratio
options.rationale: Applies the turns ratio to any supply, because the equation itself says nothing about change.

options.text: An alternating output, because transformers always give ac
options.rationale: Treats the transformer as a device that converts dc into ac.

options.text: Zero, because the field in the core is no longer changing
options.rationale: Only a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference; a steady current gives a steady field and no output.

options.text: Half the input, since only one coil is now working
options.rationale: Invents a partial output rather than recognising that nothing is induced at all.

mcqs.stem: How does an alternating current in the primary coil cause a potential difference across the secondary coil?

options.text: It makes a continually changing field in the core, which induces one
options.rationale: The alternating current produces a changing magnetic field in the core, and that changing field induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.

options.text: It drives current through the iron core into the secondary coil
options.rationale: Makes the core an electrical connection; the core carries magnetic field, not current.

options.text: It heats the core, and the warm core drives the secondary coil
options.rationale: Substitutes a thermal mechanism for electromagnetic induction.

options.text: It raises the frequency, and the higher frequency is the output
options.rationale: Has the transformer change the frequency, which it does not.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 400 on the secondary. Why does this ratio of turns produce a larger potential difference across the secondary coil?

options.text: Because the extra turns lower the resistance of the secondary coil
options.rationale: Reaches for resistance, the only coil property met before this topic, and gets its effect wrong too.

options.text: Because the same changing field cuts four times as many turns
options.rationale: Each turn of the secondary has a potential difference induced across it, and the turns are in series, so four times the turns gives four times the potential difference.

options.text: Because the potential difference is shared among the extra turns
options.rationale: Uses the everyday sharing picture, which inverts the ratio.

options.text: Because more turns means a stronger current in the primary coil
options.rationale: Explains a secondary property by changing the primary current instead.

mcqs.stem: The National Grid transmits electrical power at very high potential difference. Which statement gives the reason, using Vs x Is = Vp x Ip?

options.text: A high potential difference lowers the resistance of the long cables
options.rationale: Attaches the saving to resistance, which is fixed by the cables themselves.

options.text: For a given power a higher potential difference means a smaller current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables
options.rationale: This reasoning is correct, but the statement is not the one asked for here; it is offered as a check on careless reading.

options.text: A higher potential difference means a smaller current, so the cables waste less energy as heating
options.rationale: For a fixed power, raising the potential difference lowers the current, and a smaller current wastes less energy heating the cables.

options.text: A high potential difference raises the current, delivering more power
options.rationale: Raises both quantities together, which would break Vs x Is = Vp x Ip.
